profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting in an ML research lab between the lead author and a research associate to organize a comprehensive survey paper on deep learning in palmprint recognition. The context is that they want to submit a survey to a biometrics journal within six weeks, and they already have a rough bibliography and a previous internal slide deck on palm biometrics. The agenda is to decide the survey structure, divide writing and evidence-gathering responsibilities, and set a timeline for producing a complete first draft. The expected outcome is an agreed chapter outline, ownership of sections, and a writing schedule for the first draft and literature tables.

members.name: Dr. Lina Qureshi
members.expertise: Biometric machine learning, survey writing, research framing
members.background: Leads a university ML-for-biometrics group and has previously published survey and benchmark papers on face and fingerprint recognition, with a focus on positioning research trends and open problems for journal audiences.
members.private_state: She wants a polished survey that is broad enough to establish her lab's authority in contactless hand biometrics, and she is trying to minimize last-minute restructuring by reusing the conceptual framing from an earlier seminar deck.
hidden_assumptions: A 'comprehensive survey' should cover the full palmprint pipeline, including adjacent tasks such as ROI extraction, spoofing defense, template protection, and multimodal hand settings, even if some papers are only partly about recognition.
The 'recent literature' means roughly the deep learning era from around 2016 onward, because earlier work is only needed as light historical context.
A 'first draft' means near-submission quality prose with integrated figures, cleaned taxonomy tables, and synthesized challenge sections, not just bullet notes.
The team's old 'hand biometrics deck' is an accepted shared starting point for section framing, terminology, and task grouping.

members.name: Ethan Wu
members.expertise: Literature mining, experimental taxonomy building, biometric datasets
members.background: Recently joined from an applied vision lab where he built structured review spreadsheets and reproducibility summaries for niche recognition topics, usually producing evidence matrices before narrative writing.
members.private_state: He wants to keep the project tractable and deliver quickly by focusing on clearly DL-based palmprint recognition papers, avoiding scope creep into loosely related hand biometrics and lengthy polished writing too early.
hidden_assumptions: A 'comprehensive survey' should still stay within core palmprint recognition and only include security or ROI papers when they directly evaluate recognition performance.
The 'recent literature' means approximately the last five years, because that is the period journals expect as the actionable state of the art.
A 'first draft' means a complete structured manuscript skeleton with section text placeholders, tables, and annotated notes that can later be polished.
The relevant prior material is the lab's Zotero folder labeled 'palmprint survey seed,' not the broader hand biometrics seminar deck, which he sees as background rather than a template.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as a comprehensive survey
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the paper should be a 'comprehensive survey' covering DL-based palmprint recognition.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes this includes the full pipeline and neighboring subtopics: ROI segmentation, feature extraction, spoofing/presentation attack detection, template protection, privacy-preserving learning, and possibly multimodal palm-related systems if they inform the field.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes this should remain focused on core DL recognition papers, with ancillary topics only briefly mentioned when they directly affect recognition benchmarks.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both see themselves as advocating rigor rather than different scope; 'comprehensive' sounds mutually supportive and neither interpretation feels unusual enough to spell out in a planning meeting.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to prioritize the 'recent literature' and use older work only for context.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means papers from roughly 2016 onward, corresponding to the rise of deep learning approaches in this niche.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means mainly the last five years, around 2020 onward, with earlier DL work treated as prehistory unless especially influential.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In survey planning, 'recent' is a routine shorthand and both also mention historical context, creating the impression of alignment while the actual year cutoff remains unstated.

misalignment_points.topic: What the first draft should contain
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree on having a 'complete first draft' ready in two weeks.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 expects prose-complete sections, integrated comparison tables, finalized taxonomy, and near-camera-ready figures sufficient for a coauthor review with only moderate edits left.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 expects a full structural draft with all references inserted, section bullets expanded into rough paragraphs, and tables populated enough to guide later writing, but not polished narrative or final visuals.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both use common academic shorthand where 'first draft' often varies by seniority and workflow style; because they are discussing planning rather than reviewing an artifact, neither notices the difference in completion standard.

misalignment_points.topic: Which prior materials they will build from
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'start from the existing material' to save time.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring to her previous seminar deck on hand biometrics, whose section ordering and terminology she expects to be repurposed into the survey outline.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is referring to the shared Zotero folder and spreadsheet seed containing candidate palmprint papers, which he expects will anchor the outline and evidence tables.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both know there is some preexisting lab material and the phrase 'existing material' sounds naturally sufficient; each assumes the most salient artifact in their own workflow is the obvious shared reference.

turns.inner_thought: I need to get this scoped now so we do not end up renegotiating structure later. If we call it a comprehensive survey on DL-based palmprint recognition, that should naturally include the full pipeline and adjacent issues the journal audience will expect: acquisition and ROI, feature learning, matching, spoofing, protection, privacy, and related hand settings where useful. Also, a complete first draft in two weeks has to mean something I can circulate without embarrassment—real prose, figures, tables, a stable taxonomy. If Ethan builds from the seminar framing, we can move fast.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time, Ethan. We should lock the plan today so the survey feels comprehensive and we can move quickly toward a complete first draft. With the submission window only a few weeks out, I want the structure and ownership settled before we start writing in parallel.

turns.inner_thought: Good, if we keep this practical I can make fast progress. A comprehensive survey is fine as long as we stay centered on actual DL palmprint recognition papers and don't disappear into neighboring hand-biometrics topics. For recent literature, I'll prioritize roughly the last five years and use older work sparingly. And if we start from the existing material, the obvious base is the Zotero seed folder and spreadsheet; I can turn that into an evidence matrix quickly.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. I can structure the recent literature pretty efficiently if we start from the existing material already in the lab, then build the sections around that rather than beginning from scratch.

turns.inner_thought: I'll put the expected arc on the table without overexplaining. The survey should read like a field map: early pipeline pieces first, then recognition proper, then the security and privacy side. That's the cleanest way to repurpose the hand biometrics deck and it broadens the paper enough to position the lab well.
turns.utterance: For the outline, I’m thinking we move from the early pipeline components into the recognition sections, and then close with security- and privacy-oriented challenges so the whole paper reads as a comprehensive survey rather than just a list of models.

turns.inner_thought: That still sounds compatible with what I had in mind. I'll make sure the recognition papers remain the backbone, and I can mention side areas where they help explain benchmark results or practical constraints. As long as the center of gravity stays on recognition, this is manageable.
turns.utterance: Yes, that works. I’ll keep the core sections centered on the recognition papers and fold in the side topics where they support the main story, so the narrative stays tight while still feeling comprehensive.

turns.inner_thought: The real synthesis has to start around the deep learning transition. Pre-DL palmprint work can be handled briefly, but the field's modern shape starts around 2016, and that is where the taxonomy and open problems become meaningful.
turns.utterance: Exactly. I also want us to synthesize the recent literature carefully, because that’s really where the field takes shape for deep learning methods, with the older work serving mainly as context.

turns.inner_thought: Great, so I'll begin with the last five years and make that the actionable survey core. Then I can backfill a concise history section with a few milestone papers so reviewers don't complain that we ignored the roots. No reason to spend days on pre-2020 detail unless absolutely necessary.
turns.utterance: I can do that. I’ll assemble the recent literature tables first and then backfill a short historical context section from the older milestone papers, which should give us a clean flow.

turns.inner_thought: I'll take the challenges-and-opportunities synthesis, since that is where framing matters most. Ethan can build the dataset, architecture, and evaluation tables from the seminar-derived material once he sees the section labels. He should be able to translate the old framing into manuscript tables without much hand-holding.
turns.utterance: Let’s split it this way: I’ll take the challenges-and-opportunities narrative, and you prepare the dataset, architecture, and evaluation summary tables. Start from the existing material as the base, and then we can iterate once the backbone is visible.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect. I'll clean the Zotero seed records, deduplicate entries, tag by task and benchmark, and convert the spreadsheet into an evidence matrix that can feed the manuscript. That gives us something concrete fast, even if the prose comes later.
turns.utterance: Works for me. I’ll clean the seed records, cluster the papers by task, and turn the base material into a draftable evidence matrix so we have something solid to write from.

turns.inner_thought: I need to set expectations clearly enough on timing, even if 'complete first draft' should be obvious. In two weeks I want prose-complete sections, integrated tables, figures that won't need redoing, and enough polish to send to coauthors. We cannot hand them a scaffold.
turns.utterance: Good. Then let’s anchor on this: in two weeks we should have a complete first draft ready so I can send it to the other coauthors before the journal deadline window tightens.

turns.inner_thought: Two weeks is tight but feasible if the first draft means a full manuscript skeleton with populated sections and tables, not final prose. I can make it coherent enough for collaborative revision, but not camera-ready. She probably just wants enough completeness to circulate.
turns.utterance: Yes, that target is workable. By then I can have all sections populated, the tables mostly filled, and the manuscript coherent enough for us to revise jointly before it goes out.

turns.inner_thought: I should nudge him toward the seminar organization without turning this into a long explanation. Reusing that framing will keep terminology and transitions consistent, especially across pipeline and challenge sections, and save me from restructuring later.
turns.utterance: One other thing: let’s reuse the previous framing where we can, just to keep the terminology and section transitions consistent across the survey and avoid unnecessary churn later.

turns.inner_thought: Fine by me—I'll treat that as staying consistent with the tags and groupings already in the survey seed materials. My immediate job is still to organize the recent recognition-focused set, build the taxonomy tables, and package a usable manuscript draft for review.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. I’ll organize the recent recognition-focused papers, draft the taxonomy tables, and prepare the initial manuscript package for review, then we can tighten the framing together once the draft is in place.
